Unit 9

Segmentation & Sizing

30 minutes

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Segment markets by category, competition, growth potential, and buyer tier (SMB/Mid-market/Enterprise)
  • Build a TAM/SAM/SOM analysis using AI-assisted research and available data
  • Map customer segments by funnel stage, role, and buyer power
  • Identify buying committees and understand who influences vs. who decides

Lesson 1: Market Segmentation

Before you can position a product, enable a sales team, or run a campaign, you need to answer a deceptively simple question: who are we going after?

Market segmentation is the discipline of dividing a broad market into distinct subsets of buyers who have common needs, characteristics, or behaviors. For B2B software—especially at enterprise scale—this means thinking along three dimensions:

  1. Category view — where do we play relative to competition?
  2. Growth view — which segments are expanding vs. contracting?
  3. Buyer tier view — SMB, mid-market, or enterprise?

The Category-Competition Matrix

Every market can be mapped against two axes: how mature is the category (established vs. emerging) and how crowded is the competition (fragmented vs. consolidated). This gives you four strategic quadrants:

Fragmented Competition
Consolidated Competition
Our Opportunity
Emerging Category
🌱 Land grab — first mover wins
⚔️ Platform war — pick your battles
🎯 Define the category narrative
Established Category
🔄 Consolidation play — acquire or be acquired
🏰 Defend & expand — switching costs matter
💡 Differentiate on outcomes, not features

💡 Why This Matters for PMM

Your messaging strategy depends on which quadrant you're in. In emerging/fragmented markets, you're educating buyers on why this category matters. In established/consolidated markets, you're persuading them why you're the better choice. Same product, very different narrative.

Growth Quadrant Analysis

Not all segments deserve equal investment. The classic BCG matrix—adapted for software markets—helps you prioritize:

⭐ Stars

High growth, high share. Invest heavily—these are your future cash cows.

❓ Question Marks

High growth, low share. Decide: double down or exit? Can't stay here forever.

💰 Cash Cows

Low growth, high share. Milk for profit, fund your stars and question marks.

🐕 Dogs

Low growth, low share. Divest or harvest. Don't throw good money after bad.

🟢 SAP Context

At SAP, segmentation often maps to our industry cloud strategy. Some industries (like retail or utilities) have mature, established needs. Others (like sustainability or AI governance) are emerging. Your PMM strategy should reflect where your product sits in each industry's growth curve.

Buyer Tier Segmentation

The same product sold to a 50-person company and a 50,000-person enterprise requires completely different motions:

🏪

SMB

< $50M revenue
  • Self-serve or low-touch
  • Price-sensitive
  • Fast decisions (days/weeks)
  • 1-2 decision makers
🏢

Mid-Market

$50M - $1B revenue
  • Inside sales + partners
  • Value-conscious
  • Moderate cycles (weeks/months)
  • 3-5 decision makers
🏛️

Enterprise

> $1B revenue
  • Field sales + solutions
  • Outcome-focused
  • Long cycles (months/quarters)
  • 7-12+ decision makers

💡 The Motion Must Match the Market

Enterprise messaging emphasizes risk reduction and strategic alignment. SMB messaging emphasizes speed to value and simplicity. Mid-market is the awkward middle—too big for self-serve, too small for white-glove. Get the motion wrong and you'll burn CAC fighting the wrong battle.

Lesson 2: Building TAM with AI

Total Addressable Market (TAM) isn't just a number for investor decks—it's the foundation for territory planning, resource allocation, and strategic prioritization. But too often, TAM analysis is either hand-wavy ("it's a $50B market!") or paralyzingly complex.

AI changes that. With the right prompts and data sources, you can build defensible TAM models in hours, not weeks.

The TAM/SAM/SOM Framework

$50B TAM — Total Addressable Market
$12B SAM — Serviceable Addressable Market
$800M SOM — Serviceable Obtainable Market
  • TAM = Everyone who could theoretically buy your product category
  • SAM = The portion you can actually reach with your current go-to-market
  • SOM = What you can realistically capture given competition and resources

Data Sources for TAM Analysis

Good TAM analysis triangulates multiple data sources:

📊
Industry reports (Gartner, IDC, Forrester)
🏢
Public filings (10-K, S-1, earnings calls)
🔍
LinkedIn, ZoomInfo, company databases

AI-Assisted TAM Building

Here's how to use AI to accelerate your TAM analysis:

🤖 Sample Prompt: Top-Down TAM

I'm sizing the market for [product category] in [region/industry].

Help me build a TAM estimate using:
1. Industry analyst reports (cite Gartner, IDC, Forrester if available)
2. Public company revenue disclosures in this space
3. Growth rate projections (CAGR)

Structure the output as:
- TAM: Total market size with methodology
- Key assumptions and limitations
- 3-year projection with growth drivers

🤖 Sample Prompt: Bottom-Up TAM

Help me build a bottom-up TAM for [product] targeting [buyer persona].

Calculate:
1. Total number of target companies by segment (SMB/Mid/Enterprise)
2. Estimated # of [relevant users/seats/units] per company tier
3. Average deal size by tier based on [pricing model]
4. Multiply to get TAM, then adjust for:
   - Geographic coverage (we only sell in [regions])
   - Industry fit (we focus on [industries])
   - Tech stack requirements

Show your math at each step.

📌 Example: Sizing SAP Datasphere TAM

Top-down: IDC sizes the global data management market at $82B (2024), growing 12% CAGR. Cloud data platforms represent ~35% = $28.7B.

Bottom-up: 50,000 enterprises globally with 500+ employees × average $200K annual data platform spend × 40% addressable (right tech stack, cloud-ready) = $4B SAM.

SOM: Current market share (~8%) × growth investments = $500M realistic year target.

💡 The "So What" Test

TAM analysis isn't academic—it drives real decisions. Which segments do we prioritize? Where do we hire? Which features matter most? A good TAM model should make these tradeoffs explicit, not hide them in aggregate numbers.

Lesson 3: Customer Segmentation Deep Dive

Market segmentation tells you which companies to target. Customer segmentation tells you which people within those companies matter—and what motivates them.

At SAP scale, this means understanding three dimensions:

  1. Funnel stages — where is the buyer in their journey?
  2. Roles — who does what in the buying process?
  3. Buyer power — who decides vs. who influences?

Funnel Stage Segmentation

Different content, different channels, different messages for each stage:

🔍 Awareness Buyer recognizes a problem exists. Content: thought leadership, trends, pain points.
🤔 Consideration Buyer evaluates solution categories. Content: comparison guides, use cases, ROI frameworks.
📋 Decision Buyer compares specific vendors. Content: demos, proof points, customer references.
✍️ Purchase Buyer negotiates and procures. Content: business cases, security/compliance docs, pricing.
🚀 Adoption Buyer implements and expands. Content: onboarding, training, success stories.

🟢 SAP Funnel Reality

Enterprise deals rarely follow a linear funnel. Buyers loop back, stakeholders enter late, and procurement can restart the whole process. Smart PMMs map content to buyer needs at each stage, not just sequential steps. Build modular content that works when the CIO asks "wait, remind me why we need this?" in month six.

Role-Based Segmentation

The same product needs different messages for different roles:

Role
Cares About
Content That Works
C-Suite
Strategic outcomes, competitive advantage, risk
Executive briefings, board-ready ROI, analyst endorsements
IT/Technical
Architecture, integration, security, maintenance
Technical docs, sandbox access, reference architectures
Line of Business
Solving their specific problem, usability, speed
Use cases, demos, day-in-the-life scenarios
Procurement
Price, terms, compliance, vendor risk
Competitive pricing, certifications, legal terms

The Buying Committee: Buyers vs. Influencers

Enterprise deals involve committees, not individuals. Understanding buyer power is critical:

👔 Economic Buyer High Power

Controls the budget. Usually a VP or C-level. Can say yes when everyone else says no. Can kill deals single-handedly.

👩‍💻 Technical Buyer High Power

Validates technical fit. Can veto on architecture, security, or integration concerns. Often IT or Engineering leadership.

📊 User Buyer Medium Power

Will actually use the product. Drives adoption success. Can influence with enthusiasm or kill with indifference.

🛡️ Coach/Champion Medium Power

Your internal advocate. Sells when you're not in the room. Critical for navigating politics. Find and enable them.

📋 Procurement Gatekeeping

Manages the process, not the decision. Can slow deals but rarely kills them alone. Respect the process.

⚖️ Legal/Security Gatekeeping

Risk and compliance review. Can block deals on red flags. Front-load compliance docs to avoid late surprises.

💡 Multi-Threading is Survival

Deals that depend on a single champion are fragile. That person leaves, gets promoted, or loses influence—and your deal evaporates. Smart PMMs create content that helps sales multi-thread: reach multiple stakeholders with role-specific value props. If you're only talking to one person, you're one reorg away from starting over.

📌 Mapping a Real Deal

For a $2M SAP Datasphere deal, a typical buying committee might include:

  • Economic Buyer: CFO or CDO (approves spend, cares about business outcomes)
  • Technical Buyer: VP Data Engineering (validates architecture, integration with existing stack)
  • User Buyer: BI/Analytics team leads (will build on the platform daily)
  • Champion: Director of Data Strategy (believes in the vision, drives internal consensus)
  • Gatekeepers: Procurement, InfoSec, Legal

Your PMM job: ensure sales has the right asset for each person. Economic buyer gets ROI models. Technical buyer gets architecture docs. Users get demos. Champion gets competitive ammunition.
